hub.headerNote: No data ever leaves your browser
hub.titleHtml:
From idea to prototype,
one decision at a time.
hub.intro: Three short, independent, shareable questionnaires to guide your product decisions, no unnecessary jargon, with the methodology reference behind every recommendation.

idea.title: Does this idea deserve a discovery, or should it go straight to the backlog?
idea.description: A 5-question filter (business link, user signals, clarity of the problem and the solution) to avoid over-processing quick wins or under-exploring risky bets.

discovery.title: Which discovery artifact should you use to reduce your uncertainty?
discovery.description: OST, Story Map, JTBD, Impact Map, HMW, or Assumption Map: the right format depends on your goal, your audience, and the time available, not on personal preference.

proto.title: What type of prototype should you build to validate your hypothesis?
proto.description: Desirability, feasibility, viability, or usability: two quick questions to know whether you need a landing page, a POC, a Wizard of Oz, or a 5-second test.

hub.pipelineHtml: Idea → Discovery → Prototype: a logical pipeline, but each tool launches on its own, with its own page.
hub.footer: PM Tool Project · no data ever leaves your browser.

faq.intro: About privacy, the method, and the real usefulness of these tools.
faq.footer: PM Tool Project · no data ever leaves your browser.

items.question: Are my answers stored anywhere?
items.answerHtml: No. There's no server, no database. Your answers stay in your browser (via localStorage), just so you don't lose your progress if you close the tab. Nothing is ever sent anywhere else, and you can clear everything at any time by clearing this site's data in your browser.

items.question: Is it free? Do I need to create an account?
items.answerHtml: Free, no signup, no email. You open a page, answer, and get your recommendation.

items.question: What are the recommendations based on?
items.answerHtml: On recognized product discovery frameworks: Teresa Torres (Opportunity Solution Tree), Melissa Perri (build trap), Jeff Patton (Story Mapping), Gojko Adzic (Impact Mapping), Marty Cagan (desirability/feasibility/viability/usability), among others. Each recommendation explains its reasoning and cites its source, so you can challenge it instead of following it blindly.

items.question: Do these tools replace my judgment as a PM?
items.answerHtml: No, they help make it explicit. A 4-5 question decision tree never captures every variable of a real product decision (internal politics, deadlines, technical debt...). That's true of any framework, not just this one. What the tool brings is forcing you to clearly answer questions you often skip out of habit or overconfidence: "do I have a real user signal, or just a hunch?"

items.question: I'm already a senior PM and I know these frameworks: is this useful for me?
items.answerHtml: Probably more than you think. A pilot with 20 years of experience still reads the checklist before every takeoff, not because they forgot how to fly, but because expertise itself creates an overconfidence bias that the checklist neutralizes. Beyond that, these tools also help settle a disagreement with a stakeholder using external reasoning instead of a personal opinion, create a shared team language, or document a decision after the fact.

items.question: Are the 3 tools connected to each other?
items.answerHtml: They form a logical pipeline (idea → discovery → prototype), but each works on its own. You can land directly on a single tool without going through the others.

items.question: Is the project open source? Can I contribute?
items.answerHtml:
Yes, under the MIT license. The code, tests, and decision trees are freely available on GitHub. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

github.com/MattJCand/pm-tool-project →

items.question: I found a bug or a recommendation that doesn't hold up, what do I do?
items.answerHtml: Open an issue on GitHub with the exact answers you gave. Every branch of the decision logic is tested, so a real bug gets fixed (and re-tested) quickly.

ideaStep.question: Describe your idea in one or two sentences.
ideaStep.hint: No need to be precise — a hunch is enough to get started.
ideaStep.placeholder: E.g.: Let managers see in real time where their field technicians are...
ideaStep.privacyNote: 🔒 This stays between you and this browser: nothing is sent or stored on a server. Your text is only kept locally (localStorage) so you don't lose your progress, and it's recalled in your recommendation at the end.

business.question: Is this idea tied to an identified business objective?
business.hint: Teresa Torres: an opportunity with no link to a business outcome doesn't deserve to enter the process.

options.label: Yes, the link is clear
options.hint: I know which objective it serves

options.label: Vaguely
options.hint: I have a hunch but no explicit link

options.label: Not yet
options.hint: I don't know which objective it serves

signals.question: Do you have user signals confirming a real problem?
signals.hint: Melissa Perri: the problem must be validated before exploring solutions. A signal = direct feedback, usage data, interview, NPS...

options.label: Yes, several clear signals
options.hint: Users have explicitly expressed this problem

options.label: A few weak signals
options.hint: Some hints but no direct confirmation

options.label: No signal yet
options.hint: It's an internal hunch

problem.question: Is the problem well understood and documented?
problem.hint: Teresa Torres: before moving to solutions, the problem space must be mapped. Who's affected? In what context? How often?

options.label: Yes, we understand the problem well
options.hint: Context, impact, frequency are documented

options.label: Partially
options.hint: We have some elements but grey areas remain

options.label: No, it's still unclear
options.hint: We don't yet know what's really going on

solution.question: Do you have a clear solution in mind? And what's the estimated effort?
solution.hint: Melissa Perri: when both the problem AND the solution are clear, move to execution mode. If it's a quick win, no need for discovery.

options.label: Clear solution + small effort
options.hint: Quick win, less than a sprint

options.label: Clear solution + big effort
options.hint: We know what to do, it's a big undertaking

options.label: Vague solution
options.hint: A direction but no precise solution

options.label: No solution in mind
options.hint: We don't yet know how to solve it

no_business_link.rationale: This idea isn't yet tied to an identified business objective. Without that anchor, it can't enter the product process: it risks generating build with no measurable value.
no_business_link.reference: Based on Teresa Torres (Continuous Discovery Habits): an opportunity with no link to a business outcome has no place in the Opportunity Solution Tree.
nextSteps: Identify your team's business objective for this quarter
Reframe the idea as a user problem tied to that objective
If no link can be found, put the idea in the parking lot
Revisit it during the next planning cycle

business_vague_no_signals.rationale: The link to a business objective is only a hunch, and no user signal reinforces it. This is the riskiest combination: neither the business value nor the user need is established. Clarify one of the two before investing discovery time.
business_vague_no_signals.reference: Based on Melissa Perri (Escaping the Build Trap): with no explicit business link and no user signal, an idea remains an unanchored hypothesis, not something to act on.
nextSteps: Reframe the business link: which team objective does it precisely serve?
Failing that, look for a first user signal (quick interview, support ticket, usage data)
If neither emerges, put the idea in the parking lot
Revisit it once one of the two points is clarified

business_vague_advanced.rationale: The problem is already well understood and you're about to move toward a concrete solution (maybe even a quick win), but the link to a business objective remains a hunch, not an explicit link. Committing now risks shipping something that serves no measurable outcome, even if the problem itself is real.
business_vague_advanced.reference: Based on Teresa Torres (Continuous Discovery Habits): the business outcome is the root of the Opportunity Solution Tree. A vague link needs to be made explicit before moving forward, not just a fully missing one.
nextSteps: State in one sentence the precise business objective this idea serves
Check that link with a stakeholder or your manager before continuing
If the link holds, redo the classification with a clear business link
If it doesn't hold, send the idea back to discovery or the parking lot

double_discovery.rationale: The problem isn't validated yet and the solution remains vague. You need to explore the problem space first before looking for solutions: that's the full double diamond.
double_discovery.reference: Based on Melissa Perri: teams that jump to the solution without validating the problem fall into the build trap. Based on Teresa Torres: start by mapping opportunities before exploring solutions.
nextSteps: Phase 1 (Problem discovery): run 5 exploratory interviews on the problem
Map the opportunities with an Opportunity Solution Tree
Validate that the problem deserves to be solved (frequency, impact, current workarounds)
Phase 2 (Solution discovery): generate and test several solution directions
Prototype and validate before moving into development

discovery_solution_from_problem.rationale: The problem is understood well enough to move forward, but the solution still needs exploring. You can go straight into solution discovery without redoing problem discovery.
discovery_solution_from_problem.reference: Based on Teresa Torres: once the opportunity is well defined, the team can move directly to exploring solutions in the OST.
nextSteps: Formalize the opportunity: problem, affected users, context
Generate several solution directions (not just one)
Prototype the most promising solution(s)
Test with real users before developing

initiative.rationale: The problem is well understood, confirmed by at least one user signal, and the solution is clear. This is the right moment to move into execution mode: define the scope, align the team, and plan the development.
initiative.reference: Based on Melissa Perri: an initiative is born once you have enough clarity on the problem AND a validated solution direction.
nextSteps: Write a clear problem statement shared with the team
Define success criteria (metrics)
Break it down into deliverable steps (milestones)
Plan the sprints and align stakeholders

initiative_unvalidated.rationale: The problem seems clear to you and you're already picturing a large-scale solution, but no user signal confirms this problem for now. An undertaking of this size should never start on a mere internal hunch: validate quickly before committing the team.
initiative_unvalidated.reference: Based on Teresa Torres: never build an initiative without proof that the opportunity is real, even if it seems obvious to you.
nextSteps: Run 3 to 5 quick interviews to confirm the problem is experienced the way you imagine it
Check available usage or support data
If the problem is confirmed, redo this step with a signal filled in to launch the Initiative
If the problem isn't confirmed, re-explore solutions before committing

backlog.rationale: The solution is clear, the effort is minimal, and a user signal confirms it's worth it. No need for a full discovery phase: it's a quick win to schedule directly in the backlog.
backlog.reference: Based on Melissa Perri: quick wins with an obvious solution, low risk, and a validation signal don't need discovery. Over-processing kills velocity.
nextSteps: Write the ticket with context, acceptance criteria, and estimated effort
Prioritize it in the backlog by impact / effort
Assign it to the next available sprint
Measure the impact after delivery

backlog_quick_check.rationale: The effort is minimal and the solution seems obvious to you, but no signal yet confirms your users actually experience this problem. Even for a quick win, spending dev time with zero signal is still a bet. A light check (not a full discovery) is enough before committing.
backlog_quick_check.reference: Based on Melissa Perri: a quick win remains a bet as long as no signal, even a weak one, confirms the problem it solves.
nextSteps: Quickly check available data: support tickets, analytics, sales feedback
If possible, confirm with 1 or 2 users in a few minutes
If a signal appears, write the ticket and prioritize it in the backlog
If no signal appears, reconsider the priority of this idea

discovery_solution_clear_problem.rationale: The problem is well documented and validated by users. All that's left is finding the right solution: go straight into solution discovery without revisiting the problem.
discovery_solution_clear_problem.reference: Based on Teresa Torres: don't go back to problem discovery if the opportunity is already well defined. Focus on exploring solutions.
nextSteps: List the constraints and criteria of the ideal solution
Generate at least 3 different solution directions
Quickly prototype the most promising one
Test and iterate before committing to development

discovery_solution_weak_signals.rationale: The problem already seems clear to you, but the user signals confirming it are weak or absent, unlike a truly validated problem. Explore solutions, but do it in parallel with gathering stronger signals: don't lock anything in until the problem is confirmed from the outside.
discovery_solution_weak_signals.reference: Based on Teresa Torres: an opportunity that seems clear internally should always be cross-checked with external user signals before you invest in its solutions.
nextSteps: Generate 2 to 3 solution directions without committing to them yet
In parallel, run a few interviews or check the data to confirm the problem
Prioritize the most promising direction once the problem is confirmed
Prototype and test before developing

goal.question: What's your main goal right now?
goal.hint: Each artifact has a precise function. Picking the wrong tool for the right moment is still the wrong choice.

options.label: Understand the problem
options.hint: Explore user needs, pain points, and context

options.label: Explore solutions
options.hint: Generate and prioritize solution directions

options.label: Align the team or stakeholders
options.hint: Create a shared vision of the problem or product

options.label: Plan the delivery of a known solution
options.hint: Break down and sequence what you'll build

clarity.question: Where are you in your understanding of the problem?
clarity.hint: Teresa Torres: before exploring solutions, the opportunity space needs to be sufficiently mapped.

options.label: Starting from scratch
options.hint: No clarity yet on the problem or the users

options.label: I have hypotheses
options.hint: I think I understand the problem but it needs validating

options.label: The problem is well understood
options.hint: Validated by clear user signals

options.label: Both problem AND solution are clear
options.hint: I know what we're building, it needs planning

audience.question: Who are you building this artifact for?
audience.hint: A solo artifact structures your thinking. A collective artifact creates alignment. The two have very different formats.

options.label: Just for me
options.hint: Structuring my thinking

options.label: Product team
options.hint: Dev, design, PM

options.label: Business stakeholders
options.hint: Leadership, business, clients

options.label: Everyone
options.hint: Company-wide alignment

horizon.question: What horizon are you working on?
horizon.hint: The horizon determines the level of abstraction of the artifact: from ticket to product vision.

options.label: Short term · a feature or a sprint
options.hint: A few weeks

options.label: Medium term · a product or a release
options.hint: A few months

options.label: Long term · vision or strategy
options.hint: 6 months to several years

depth.question: How much time can you spend on this discovery?
depth.hint: Available budget changes the nature of the artifact: a light format if you need to move fast, a full format if you have the bandwidth to map things in depth.

options.label: Little time
options.hint: A few hours to a day, I need to move fast

options.label: Plenty of time ahead
options.hint: Several days, I can map things in depth

overrides.plan_delivery_contradiction: You want to plan a delivery, but the problem isn't understood at all yet: planning now would mean sequencing work on an uncertain base. Start by framing the problem with a HMW / Problem Statement, then come back to plan once you have clarity.
overrides.align_team_solo_contradiction: You want to align the team, but you said you're working alone: an alignment artifact assumes an audience to convince, so this combination doesn't match a real need. Here's an individual clarification artifact instead; come back and pick a real audience (team, stakeholders, everyone) once you actually want to align someone.

ost.name: Opportunity Solution Tree
ost.author: Teresa Torres, Continuous Discovery Habits
ost.rationale: The OST is the central artifact of discovery. It structures the relationship between your business outcome, user opportunities, possible solutions, and the experiments to run. It keeps you from jumping to a solution before mapping the problem space.
ost.reference: Based on Teresa Torres: the OST forces you to stay connected to the business outcome while systematically exploring the opportunity space. It's a living map, not a fixed deliverable.
nextSteps: Put your business outcome at the top of the tree
List all opportunities (needs, pains, desires) without judging
Group and prioritize opportunities by impact
For each priority opportunity, generate several solutions
Identify the hypotheses to test first
also: Story Mapping (if you move into delivery)
ProtoAdvisor (once a direction is prioritized, choose how to validate it before building)

story_map.name: Story Mapping
story_map.author: Jeff Patton, User Story Mapping
story_map.rationale: The Story Map lets you visualize the full user journey and sequence the features to build. It's the ideal tool once the problem is understood and you need to plan what you'll build, and in what order.
story_map.reference: Based on Jeff Patton: a story map puts every user story back into its context of use. It shows the big picture that flat backlogs make disappear.
nextSteps: Identify the major user activities (horizontal axis)
Break down each activity into detailed tasks
Prioritize vertically: what's essential vs what can wait
Draw a horizontal line to define your MVP
Align the team on the minimal slice to ship first
also: OST (if pockets of uncertainty come up)
ProtoAdvisor (to validate each slice before building it for real)

impact_map.name: Impact Mapping
impact_map.author: Gojko Adzic, Impact Mapping
impact_map.rationale: The Impact Map aligns features with business objectives by asking four questions: Why? (goal) Who? (actors) How? (impacts) What? (deliverables). It's the perfect artifact to align business stakeholders and the product team on priorities.
impact_map.reference: Based on Gojko Adzic: the Impact Map keeps you from building features disconnected from objectives. It forces the conversation about expected impact before talking about solutions.
nextSteps: Define the measurable business objective at the center
Identify the actors who can help you reach it
For each actor, describe the expected behavioral impact
List the deliverables that could create that impact
Prioritize the branches with the strongest leverage on the objective
also: OST (to go deeper on opportunities once deliverables are identified)
ProtoAdvisor (once a direction is prioritized, choose how to validate it before building)

hmw.name: How Might We + Problem Statement
hmw.author: IDEO, Design Thinking
hmw.rationale: HMW reframes a problem as an invitation to explore. It's the starting artifact when you're beginning from scratch: it opens up the space of possibilities without forcing a solution. A good Problem Statement frames what you're trying to solve without dictating how.
hmw.reference: Based on IDEO: the quality of your solution depends directly on the quality of your question. A well-formed HMW generates more relevant ideas than a technical brief.
nextSteps: Gather raw observations about the problem (interviews, data)
Reframe each problem as 'How might we...?'
Generate several framings of the same problem (broader, narrower)
Pick the framing that opens up without constraining
Use it as a starting point for the OST or the Impact Map
also: OST (natural next step once the problem is better framed)
Assumption Mapping (to test your problem hypotheses)
ProtoAdvisor (once a direction is prioritized, choose how to validate it before building)

jtbd.name: Jobs To Be Done: Job Story
jtbd.author: Clayton Christensen (Jobs To Be Done theory), Job Story format by Alan Klement
jtbd.rationale: JTBD identifies what the user is really trying to accomplish, independent of any solution. It reveals deep motivations where user stories stay on the surface. It's the ideal artifact to understand why people use (or don't use) your product.
jtbd.reference: Based on Clayton Christensen: customers don't buy products, they 'hire' them to get a job done. Understanding the job means understanding the real competition. The writing format used here ('When I... I want to... so that...') is the Job Story format by Alan Klement, a lightweight reformulation of JTBD theory — not to be confused with Tony Ulwick's 8-step Job Map (define/locate/prepare/confirm/execute/monitor/modify/conclude).
nextSteps: Write the main job as a Job Story: 'When I... I want to... so that...'
Map the functional, emotional, and social jobs
Identify current frictions (pain points) in getting the job done
Look for existing workarounds: they reveal the real needs
Prioritize the underserved jobs with the strongest potential
also: OST (to explore solutions once the job is clarified)
ProtoAdvisor (once a direction is prioritized, choose how to validate it before building)

assumption_map.name: Assumption Mapping
assumption_map.author: David Bland & Alex Osterwalder, Testing Business Ideas
assumption_map.rationale: The Assumption Map identifies and prioritizes your idea's critical assumptions along two dimensions: importance to success and current level of certainty. It tells you what to test first, before investing in development.
assumption_map.reference: Based on David Bland & Alex Osterwalder: every product idea rests on assumptions. Teams that fail are the ones that build without having identified and tested their riskiest assumptions.
nextSteps: List all the assumptions behind your idea (desirability, feasibility, viability)
Place each assumption on the matrix: importance × certainty
Identify the 'important + uncertain' quadrant: those are your testing priorities
Define an experiment to test each critical assumption
Start with the riskiest assumption, not the easiest
also: OST (to feed the results back in once assumptions are tested)
ProtoAdvisor (once a direction is prioritized, choose how to validate it before building)

hypothesisStep.question: What's the hypothesis you want to validate?
hypothesisStep.placeholder: E.g.: Managers would pay for a real-time dashboard tracking their field technicians...
hypothesisStep.privacyNote: 🔒 Nothing is sent to a server: your text stays local to this browser and will be recalled in your recommendation.

risk.question: What's the main risk in this hypothesis?

options.label: Desirability
options.hint: Do people actually want it?

options.label: Feasibility
options.hint: Can we build it?

options.label: Viability
options.hint: Is it profitable for the business?

options.label: Usability
options.hint: Will they know how to use it?

need.question: What do you need to validate it?

desirability.label: A reaction without building the real system
desirability.hint: Simulate it to observe the real reaction

desirability.label: An intent signal (not a purchase yet)
desirability.hint: Click on a feature that doesn't exist yet

feasibility.label: A built technical proof
feasibility.hint: A POC that answers the question

viability.label: An opinion from a business decision-maker

framework.author: Marty Cagan, SVPG (desirability / feasibility / viability / usability framework)
framework.reference: Based on Marty Cagan (Silicon Valley Product Group): a prototype only ever validates one thing at a time (desirability, feasibility, viability, or usability). These are the same four risks evaluated in DiscoveryAdvisor and IdeaClassifier, seen here from the angle of validation rather than exploration.

behavior.name: Landing Page
behavior.rationale: You want to know if people click, sign up, take action. A landing page with a clear CTA will give you real data in 24-48h without building anything.
nextSteps: Write a clear one-line promise
Build the landing page with a CTA (button, form)
Drive traffic to it (5-10 people from your target)
Measure the click / signup rate

qualitative.name: Interview script
qualitative.rationale: Before building anything, talk to 5 people. A good interview script will reveal whether the problem is real and whether your solution resonates, without writing a line of code.
nextSteps: Prepare 5-7 open-ended questions about the problem (not the solution)
Recruit 5 people from your exact target
Run the interviews, 30 min each
Look for recurring patterns in the answers

technical.name: Wizard of Oz
technical.rationale: Simulate the system manually behind a simple interface. The user thinks it's automated, you do everything by hand. You validate desirability before investing in dev.
nextSteps: Build a minimal interface (Figma, no-code)
Perform the 'automatic' actions manually behind the scenes
Observe how users interact
Decide whether it's worth automating

intent.name: Fake Door
intent.rationale: Add a button or option that doesn't exist yet in your product. Measure how many people click on it. It's the most honest intent signal there is.
nextSteps: Identify where to place the 'fake door' in your current product
Add the button / link with a 'Coming soon' message
Measure the click rate over 1-2 weeks
Analyze who clicks (segment, usage...)

behavior.name: Technical spike
behavior.rationale: Code a throwaway prototype focused on the most technically risky part. No need for UI, no need for it to be clean, just prove it works.
nextSteps: Identify the most critical technical risk
Code the minimum to test that specific point
Set a strict timebox (1-3 days max)
Document what you learned, not what you built

qualitative.name: Technical discussion
qualitative.rationale: Before coding, talk to engineers or domain experts. A 30-minute conversation can save you weeks of development in the wrong direction.
nextSteps: Prepare your precise technical questions
Involve 1-2 devs or experts right now
Map out dependencies and potential blockers
Decide on a go / no-go before starting

technical.name: POC (Proof of Concept)
technical.rationale: A POC targeted at the most technically uncertain point. The goal isn't to have something polished, it's to answer 'can we actually do this?'
nextSteps: Define the exact technical question to answer
Build the most minimal POC possible
Test in conditions close to real ones
Document the remaining limits and risks

intent.name: Quick estimate
intent.rationale: Estimate the build cost before validating demand. Sometimes the real risk is that the build cost exceeds what customers would pay.
nextSteps: Do a rough dev cost estimate (T-shirt sizing)
Compare it with the realistic potential revenue
Identify the critical assumptions in your calculation
Validate the most uncertain assumptions first

behavior.name: Concierge MVP
behavior.rationale: Deliver the service manually, by hand, while openly presenting it as a non-automated service (unlike a Wizard of Oz, the user knows it's manual). Test the business model before building the infrastructure: if people pay for an openly manual service, they'll pay for the automated version.
nextSteps: Define your pricing hypothesis
Deliver the offer by hand, at that price, being transparent about the manual side
Find 3-5 potential customers and pitch it to them
Measure the real willingness to pay

qualitative.name: Economic interview
qualitative.rationale: Talk to decision-makers, not users. Business questions (budget, purchasing process, current alternatives) reveal whether your model holds up.
nextSteps: Identify who controls the budget at your target
Prepare questions about current costs and expected ROI
Explore the purchasing decision process
Validate your pricing and distribution channel

technical.name: Costed business case
technical.rationale: Build a simple financial model with your most uncertain assumptions. The goal is to identify the levers that make or break viability.
nextSteps: Model your revenue and cost assumptions
Identify the 2-3 most sensitive assumptions
Test those assumptions first
Define your minimum viability threshold

intent.name: Landing Page + Pricing
intent.rationale: A landing page with a real displayed price and a 'Buy' or 'Book' button will give you the most honest signal on willingness to pay.
nextSteps: Build a landing page with your clear value proposition
Display your real price (not 'contact us')
Add a purchase or booking CTA
Measure the conversion rate on your target

behavior.name: User test on a Figma prototype
behavior.rationale: Create a clickable prototype in Figma and watch real users navigate through it. You'll spot friction points before writing a line of code.
nextSteps: Create a Figma prototype of the main screens
Define 2-3 tasks for them to complete
Observe 5 users in silence (don't help them)
Note where they get stuck, hesitate, or make mistakes

qualitative.name: 5-second test
qualitative.rationale: Show your interface to someone for 5 seconds. Ask them what they remember and what they'd do. You'll immediately know whether your UX is clear or confusing.
nextSteps: Prepare a screenshot of your main interface
Show it for 5 seconds to 5-10 people
Ask: 'What is this product? What would you do?'
Identify recurring misunderstandings

technical.name: No-code interactive prototype
technical.rationale: Build a lightweight functional version with no-code tools. This lets you test real interactions without dev cost.
nextSteps: Pick a suitable no-code tool (Bubble, Webflow, Glide...)
Build only the 2-3 critical flows
Test with real users from your target
Iterate quickly on friction points

intent.name: Card sorting test
intent.rationale: Have users sort cards representing your features. You'll discover their mental model, essential before deciding your product's information architecture.
nextSteps: List your features / content on cards
Ask 5 users to group them however feels natural
Compare their groupings with your current logic
Restructure your IA based on their mental models
